title: Daredevils and Record-Breakers
summary: In 1909 a French pilot with a hurt foot flew a tiny plane across the sea from France to England in about 37 minutes. Soon there were huge air shows, brave women pilots, planes that took off from water and ships, and even the very first airline ticket. In just five years, flying went from a crazy stunt to something people could buy a seat on.

sections.heading: Dawn on the Cliffs of Calais
paragraphs: Imagine standing on a windy beach in northern France just before sunrise on Sunday, 25 July 1909. The sky is pale grey. A small crowd of mechanics, friends and reporters huddles around a strange little machine parked on a farm field at Les Baraques, between Calais and Sangatte. It looks more like a giant dragonfly than anything that should cross an ocean: one pair of cloth-covered wings, an open frame of wooden struts and wires behind them, and a tiny tail at the back. This is the Blériot XI, and its pilot, Louis Blériot, is 37 years old, limping on a foot burned in an earlier crash, and about to try something no one has ever done.

Blériot was not a beginner hoping for luck. He was a wealthy engineer who had made his fortune selling bright acetylene headlamps for early motor cars, and then spent much of that fortune building one flying machine after another. Many of them crashed. Some never left the ground. Type XI was his eleventh main design, and it was a monoplane, which means a plane with a single main wing rather than the two stacked wings of a biplane. Its engine came from the Italian-born engine maker Alessandro Anzani: a small three-cylinder motor of roughly 25 horsepower, about twice what the Wright brothers had in 1903, and still less than a modern ride-on lawnmower.

Why cross the English Channel at all? Because a London newspaper, the Daily Mail, had offered a prize of 1,000 pounds, a huge sum at the time, to the first person to fly a heavier-than-air machine across it. The newspaper's owner, Lord Northcliffe, loved bold publicity stunts, and he also wanted to wake Britain up to the coming age of flight. The narrowest part of the Channel, the Strait of Dover, is only about 34 kilometres wide, but in 1909 that was a frightening distance to fly over open water. Engines often stopped without warning, and there was nowhere to land except the waves.

Blériot was not even the favourite. That honour belonged to Hubert Latham, an elegant, daring Frenchman flying the beautiful Antoinette monoplane. On 19 July Latham had set off first, but his engine failed about 10 kilometres from Dover, and his plane glided down onto the sea. Rescuers in a French destroyer reportedly found him sitting calmly on the floating wreck, smoking a cigarette. While Latham waited for a replacement aircraft and better weather, Blériot moved in.

At 4:41 in the morning, after a short test hop, Blériot opened the throttle, bounced across the grass, and climbed out over the cliff edge and the sea. He had no compass. A French navy destroyer, the Escopette, steamed below as an escort, with his wife Alice on board, but his little plane quickly left it behind. For around ten minutes he later said he could see nothing at all: no ship, no France, no England, only grey water and grey sky. Imagine sitting in that open seat with the wind whipping your face, the engine rattling in front of you, trusting that the motor would keep going for just a few more minutes.

The wind pushed him east of his planned course. When the white cliffs finally appeared, he turned and followed the coast until he spotted a French journalist waving a large flag on the clifftop near Dover Castle, marking a dip in the cliffs called Northfall Meadow. Blériot cut the engine and dropped in rather hard. The landing gear was damaged and one propeller blade broke, but he climbed out unhurt. The flight had taken about 37 minutes (36 minutes and 30 seconds by most records).

sections.heading: Britain Is No Longer an Island
paragraphs: Within hours the news raced around the world by telegraph. Blériot was greeted in London by huge crowds, and his little monoplane was put on display at the Selfridges department store, where thousands of people queued to see it. Orders for copies of the Type XI flooded into his workshop. Between 1909 and 1914 his company built roughly 900 aircraft, most of them versions of the Type XI. A plane that had nearly bankrupted him turned him into one of the world's leading aircraft makers.

But not everyone in Britain was simply cheering. For hundreds of years, the English Channel had protected Britain from invasion. The Spanish Armada had failed to cross it in 1588. Napoleon had gathered an army on these same French cliffs around 1804 and never managed to cross. The Royal Navy was the most powerful in the world, and as long as it controlled the sea, Britain felt safe. Now one man in a fragile machine of wood, wire and fabric had simply flown over the top in about half an hour.

Newspaper writers quickly drew the lesson. Several commentators, including the writer H. G. Wells, argued that from a military point of view Britain was no longer an untouchable island. They were thinking far ahead: in 1909 no plane could carry a useful load of soldiers or weapons, and Blériot could barely carry himself. Yet the direction was clear. If machines kept improving at this speed, the sea would no longer be a wall. Within just a few years, as Part 13 will show, airplanes would be flying over battlefields.

Blériot's crossing also changed how ordinary people thought about flight. The Wrights had flown longer and more skilfully in 1908, but their flights were circles over fields. Blériot had gone somewhere: from one country to another, over the sea, like a ship or a train but much faster. Flying was no longer just an amazing trick. It looked like a new way to travel. That idea would take more than a decade to come true for passengers, but it began on that clifftop at Dover. Today a granite outline of his plane, set into the grass, marks the spot where he landed.

sections.heading: Champagne Country Hosts the World's First Great Air Show
paragraphs: Only a month later, an even bigger spectacle took place. From 22 to 29 August 1909, the world's best pilots gathered on the plain of Bétheny, about 5 kilometres north of the French city of Reims. The event was called the Grande Semaine d'Aviation de la Champagne, which means the Great Aviation Week of the Champagne region. The famous champagne-making companies of the area paid for it, hoping to show off their region and their wine. Historians usually call it the first big international public air meet.

Picture the scene. Grandstands, restaurants, a post office and even a special railway station had been built on the open fields. Flags fluttered above wooden sheds where the planes were kept. Over the week, around half a million visitors came to watch, including the President of France, Armand Fallières, and the British politician David Lloyd George. For most of them, it was the first time they had ever seen an airplane fly. Thirty-eight aircraft were entered, and 23 actually got into the air, which was a remarkable number in an age when engines failed constantly.

Prizes were offered for speed, distance, altitude and carrying passengers. Henri Farman, an English-born Frenchman, won the distance prize by flying about 180 kilometres in roughly three hours, circling the course again and again until his fuel ran low. Hubert Latham, the Channel swimmer of July, won the altitude prize by climbing to about 155 metres, which seemed dizzyingly high at the time. Modern airliners cruise around 70 times higher.

The most exciting race was the Gordon Bennett Cup, a speed contest for two laps of the 10-kilometre course. The only American taking part was Glenn Curtiss, the motorcycle racer and engine builder you met in Part 10. He had brought one small biplane with a powerful engine he had built himself. Blériot flew a bigger new monoplane and was the favourite. Curtiss finished the two laps in 15 minutes and 50.4 seconds, an average of about 75 kilometres per hour. Blériot followed him, and when his time was announced he had lost by less than 6 seconds. Curtiss became world famous overnight.

Reims also showed the dangers and difficulties of early flying. The airfield was ordinary farmland with haystacks, and a few planes crashed into them. On the final day, Blériot's aircraft crashed and caught fire, though he escaped with burns. Many machines spent more time being repaired than flying. Engineers noticed that the biggest problem was not wings or controls any more, but unreliable engines. That made one newcomer especially important: the Gnome rotary engine, a light and surprisingly dependable motor that made its public debut at Reims. You will learn how this odd spinning engine worked in Part 12.

sections.heading: Women Take the Controls
paragraphs: In 1909 many people believed that flying was far too dangerous and technical for women. Two remarkable pilots proved them wrong almost immediately.

The first was a Frenchwoman born Élise Deroche in Paris in 1882. She had been an actress and loved fast new things like motor cars and ballooning. Performing under the stage name Raymonde de Laroche, she became friends with the aircraft builder Charles Voisin, who agreed to teach her to fly. On 22 October 1909, at Châlons in eastern France, she took a Voisin biplane into the air and flew about 270 metres. Her teachers had reportedly told her only to taxi along the ground, but she decided she was ready. Accounts of that day differ, which is common for early aviation stories, but her skill soon became undeniable.

On 8 March 1910 the Aéro-Club de France gave her pilot licence number 36. That made her the first woman in the world to hold an official pilot's licence. Newspapers began calling her Baroness de Laroche, a grand-sounding title she did not actually hold, and the name stuck. She flew at air meets in Egypt, Russia and Hungary, where Tsar Nicholas II of Russia personally congratulated her. Flying was risky, though. In July 1910 she was badly injured in a crash at the Reims air meet, and it took her a long time to recover. She kept going. In 1913 she won the Femina Cup, a prize for women pilots, with a nonstop flight of more than four hours, and in June 1919 she set a women's altitude record of about 4,800 metres. Sadly, a few weeks later, in July 1919, she died in a crash while flying as co-pilot in an experimental plane at Le Crotoy in France. She had hoped to become one of the first women test pilots.

Across the Atlantic, Harriet Quimby was a journalist and screenwriter in New York, writing theatre reviews and travel stories for a popular magazine called Leslie's Illustrated Weekly. In 1910 she watched an air meet on Long Island and decided she had to learn to fly. She took lessons at a flying school run by the Moisant family, sometimes practising at dawn when the air was calmest. On 1 August 1911 the Aero Club of America granted her a pilot's licence, making her the first American woman to earn one. Quimby designed her own flying suit of plum-coloured satin with a hood, which could be buttoned to turn into a skirt when she was on the ground. Photographers loved it, and she became one of the most famous women in America.

Quimby wanted to be the first woman to fly across the English Channel. She borrowed a Blériot monoplane and, on 16 April 1912, took off from Dover, flying the route in the opposite direction from Blériot. The weather was cold and misty. She had never flown this particular machine before and had only a compass to guide her through the clouds. About 59 minutes later she landed on a beach at Équihen, on the French coast near Boulogne, where astonished local fishermen ran out to greet her.

Her timing could not have been worse. Just the day before, the world had learned that the great ocean liner Titanic had sunk on its first voyage. Newspapers were full of that terrible disaster, and Quimby's achievement was printed in small stories on the inside pages. Less than three months later, on 1 July 1912, she was flying at an air meet near Boston with a passenger when her plane suddenly pitched forward. Neither of them was wearing a seat belt, which was normal at that time, and both were thrown out and killed. She was 37. Her death, like many others of the era, slowly helped convince pilots that safety belts and careful design mattered.

De Laroche and Quimby were not the only ones. Women such as Hélène Dutrieu of Belgium, Lydia Zvereva of Russia and Hilda Hewlett of Britain also earned licences in these years. Hilda Hewlett even co-founded a flying school and an aircraft factory. Their courage opened a door that later pilots, including Bessie Coleman and Amelia Earhart in Part 13, would walk through.

sections.heading: Taking Off From Water and From Ships
paragraphs: Most of the Earth is covered by water, so it was natural for inventors to wonder: could a plane take off from a lake or the sea? On 28 March 1910, a French engineer named Henri Fabre answered yes. On the Étang de Berre, a large saltwater lagoon near Marseille in southern France, he climbed into a strange machine he called the Hydravion, French for water-plane. Instead of wheels it had three flat floats, and its tail was at the front, a design sometimes called a canard, which is French for duck. It was powered by a 50-horsepower Gnome rotary engine. Fabre skimmed across the water and lifted off, making four flights that day, the longest about 600 metres. Remarkably, he is reported to have had little or no experience as a pilot beforehand.

Fabre's Hydravion is often called the first true seaplane, and the original machine still survives at the Musée de l'Air et de l'Espace near Paris. His patented floats were soon used by other builders, including Glenn Curtiss in the United States, who developed practical flying boats in 1911 and 1912. Fabre himself lived an extraordinarily long life: he died in 1984 at the age of 101, after seeing jet airliners and men walking on the Moon.

Navies around the world were watching closely. If a plane could fly from a warship, it could scout far over the horizon, spotting enemy ships long before they came into view. The United States Navy decided to try. On 14 November 1910, at Hampton Roads in Virginia, carpenters built a sloping wooden platform over the front of the cruiser USS Birmingham. Eugene Ely, a 24-year-old pilot who flew for Glenn Curtiss, sat at the top of the ramp in a Curtiss pusher biplane, so called because its propeller was behind the pilot and pushed the plane forward.

The weather was poor, and Ely decided to go before it got worse, even though the ship was still at anchor. He rolled down the short ramp and over the bow. The plane dipped so low that its wheels touched the water, and spray splashed over his goggles. Somehow the engine kept running and the plane climbed away. Unable to see clearly, Ely flew to the nearest shore and landed on a beach instead of the navy yard he had planned to reach. He had made the first takeoff of an airplane from a ship.

Two months later, on 18 January 1911, he tried something even harder: landing on a ship. The cruiser USS Pennsylvania, anchored in San Francisco Bay, was fitted with a wooden deck over its stern. Across the deck, workers stretched a row of ropes, each weighted at both ends with sandbags. Hooks under Ely's plane caught the ropes as he touched down, and the dragging sandbags slowed him to a stop. He then turned the plane around and took off again. This simple idea, the tailhook and arresting wires, is the ancestor of the system modern aircraft carriers still use to stop jets in just a couple of seconds.

Like many pilots of his generation, Ely did not live long. He died in October 1911 when his plane failed to pull out of a dive during an exhibition in Macon, Georgia. He was only 24, just two days short of his 25th birthday.

sections.heading: Coast to Coast in the Vin Fiz
paragraphs: In 1911 the newspaper owner William Randolph Hearst offered 50,000 dollars to the first person to fly across the United States, from coast to coast, in less than 30 days. At that time, the longest flights lasted a few hours. America is over 4,000 kilometres wide, with mountains, deserts and very few places to buy aviation fuel or spare parts.

Calbraith Perry Rodgers decided to try. He was a tall, cigar-smoking member of a famous naval family who had learned to fly at the Wright brothers' school in Dayton only a few months earlier. He bought a Wright Model EX biplane and found a sponsor, the meatpacking businessman J. Ogden Armour, who was launching a new grape-flavoured soft drink called Vin Fiz. In return for money, Rodgers named his plane the Vin Fiz and painted advertisements on it. A special train followed him across the country, with a sleeping car, a dining car and a workshop car crammed with spare parts. Riding along as chief mechanic was none other than Charlie Taylor, the man who had built the Wright brothers' first engine in 1903.

Rodgers took off from Sheepshead Bay in Brooklyn, New York, on 17 September 1911. Almost immediately, things began to go wrong. He crashed again and again: into trees, chicken coops, fences and fields. Each time, the train crew rebuilt the plane, sometimes nearly from scratch. Engines failed. Storms forced him down. The 30-day deadline passed while he was still in the middle of the country, so he lost any chance at Hearst's prize. He kept going anyway, saying he wanted to prove it could be done.

Following railway tracks to find his way, Rodgers made around 70 stops. He finally landed at Pasadena, California, on 5 November 1911, where a cheering crowd welcomed him. The journey had taken 49 days, though he had spent only a few days' worth of hours actually in the air, often reported as about 82 hours. Weeks later, after another bad crash that put him in hospital, he flew on to Long Beach with his crutches, it is often said, strapped to the plane, and, on 10 December 1911, rolled the wheels of the Vin Fiz into the Pacific Ocean. So many parts had been replaced along the way that, according to a story often told, only a few original pieces, such as the rudder, made it all the way across.

Rodgers had made the first flight across the United States, but it also showed how far airplanes still had to go. A train could make the same trip in about four days. Sadly, in April 1912, Rodgers was killed when his plane hit a flock of seagulls and crashed into the sea at Long Beach, close to where his great journey had ended. The Vin Fiz, rebuilt again, is now in the collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

sections.heading: Look, No Hands: The First Autopilot
paragraphs: Early airplanes were exhausting to fly. They wobbled with every gust of wind, and the pilot had to make constant small corrections with the controls, hour after hour. One young American had an idea: what if a machine could do some of that work?

Lawrence Sperry was the son of Elmer Sperry, an inventor who had built gyrocompasses for ships. A gyroscope is a fast-spinning wheel that strongly resists being tilted, so it can act as a steady reference that always knows which way is level, even when everything around it is bouncing. Lawrence, who learned to fly as a teenager, worked with his father to connect gyroscopes to a plane's controls. If the plane started to tip, the gyroscopes sensed the change and moved the control surfaces to bring it back to level, using power from the plane itself rather than the pilot's muscles.

In June 1914, Lawrence Sperry, then only 21, brought his invention to an aviation safety competition near Paris, on the River Seine. Flying a Curtiss flying boat low past the judges and the crowd, he lifted his hands off the controls and held them in the air. Then his French mechanic, named in accounts as Emil Cachin, climbed out of the cockpit and walked along the wing. Normally, a man's weight shifting onto one wing would make a plane roll over. Instead, the gyroscopic stabilizer quietly adjusted the controls, and the plane stayed level. Next, Sperry himself stood up in the cockpit while the plane flew on steadily. The crowd was astonished, and Sperry won the competition's top prize, reported as 50,000 francs.

This was the ancestor of the modern autopilot. Today, autopilots fly most of a typical airliner's journey while pilots monitor the systems, and as Part 19 will show, some can even land the plane in fog. Lawrence Sperry also helped develop instruments that let pilots fly in clouds, including an early artificial horizon. Sadly, he too died young: in December 1923 he set off to fly across the English Channel in a small plane in fog and never arrived.

sections.heading: Tickets Please: The World's First Airline
paragraphs: By 1913, airplanes had crossed seas, countries and a continent. But could anyone simply buy a ticket and fly somewhere, like taking a train? In Florida, a businessman named Percival Fansler thought they could. The cities of St. Petersburg and Tampa sat on opposite sides of Tampa Bay. By steamboat the trip took about two hours, and by train it could take anywhere from about four to twelve hours because the railway went all the way around the bay. Across the water, it was only about 37 kilometres.

Fansler teamed up with Thomas Benoist, an aircraft builder from St. Louis, who had designed a small flying boat called the Benoist XIV. It had a boat-shaped hull that floated on water, a biplane wing above, and room for the pilot and one passenger side by side in an open cockpit. The city of St. Petersburg agreed to help pay for the service. It was named the St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line.

On the morning of 1 January 1914, about 3,000 people gathered at the waterfront in St. Petersburg. The first seat had been auctioned, and the winning bid of 400 dollars came from Abram C. Pheil, a former mayor of the city. That was an enormous amount, several months of wages for an ordinary worker in 1914. The pilot was Tony Jannus, a skilled 24-year-old flyer. At 10 o'clock the airboat skimmed across the water, lifted off, and flew low over the bay. About 23 minutes later it landed in Tampa. The world's first scheduled airline flight, using a winged airplane, had arrived.

After the first day, the normal fare was 5 dollars for a one-way trip, with extra charges reported for heavier passengers and baggage. The airboats made two round trips a day, and a second plane was added. Over about four months, the line carried 1,205 passengers on 172 flights without a single serious injury. When the winter tourist season ended and the city's money ran out, the service stopped in May 1914.

It was a tiny business, but it showed something huge: that ordinary people would pay to save time by flying. Earlier, German airships run by the company DELAG had carried paying passengers on pleasure trips, but the Airboat Line was the first regular, timetabled airline using airplanes. Today a memorial in St. Petersburg honours that first flight. About a century later, airlines were carrying more than four billion passengers a year.

In only five years, between 1909 and 1914, airplanes had gone from fragile machines that could barely circle a field to aircraft that crossed seas, took off from water and ships, flew across a continent and carried paying passengers. Pilots had learned a great deal. But how exactly did they steer these machines, climbing, diving and turning through the three-dimensional ocean of the sky? Up, down, left, right, tilting and twisting, what was actually happening at the controls? That is the subject of Part 12.

deepDive: Why did aviation explode between 1909 and 1914? Historians point to several overlapping forces. First, prize money. Newspapers such as the Daily Mail and the Hearst papers offered awards that could equal many years of a worker's pay, and air meets offered appearance fees and trophies. Prizes rewarded clear, measurable goals: cross this strait, beat this time, reach this height. That pushed designers toward reliability and speed rather than just getting off the ground. Second, engines. The Gnome Omega rotary of 1909 delivered about 50 horsepower for roughly 75 kilograms, a far better power-to-weight ratio than most earlier motors, and it was reliable enough to keep running for hours. Third, copying and competition. Once Blériot's Type XI was a proven design, hundreds were built and flown by others, and its layout (tractor propeller at the front, monoplane wing, tail at the back) became a template for future planes. At the same time, the Wright brothers' broad 1906 patent on lateral control led to lawsuits against Curtiss, Blériot and other builders. French and German courts largely rejected the Wrights' claims, but in the United States the legal fight is often said to have slowed American aviation until the government arranged a patent pool during World War I. By 1914, Europe, especially France, led the world in aircraft production. The human cost was high. Many of the pioneers in this part died in crashes within a few years: Ely in 1911, Rodgers and Quimby in 1912, de Laroche in 1919, Sperry in 1923. Early planes had no seat belts, no parachutes, weak structures and unreliable engines, and pilots learned largely by trial and error. Each accident taught something, and gradually safety belts, stronger structures, better training and pilot licensing became standard. A common historians' debate is about the 'first airline'. The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line is widely recognised as the first scheduled airline using fixed-wing aircraft, but the German airship company DELAG carried paying passengers from 1910, and the airlines that lasted, like KLM, did not appear until after World War I.
funFact: When Harriet Quimby became the first woman to fly across the English Channel in April 1912, hardly anyone noticed, because the news of the Titanic sinking had broken the day before.

check.q: Who flew the first scheduled airline flight in an airplane, across Tampa Bay on 1 January 1914?
